foundations.quizTarget: Change Ready to Changed, save, and run the same Rscript command again. Which message is produced?

essentialSupport.fact: Save the example as main.R and run Rscript --vanilla main.R. --vanilla avoids saved-workspace restoration and startup-profile customization; it does not install packages or make every external dependency identical.
cat writes supplied values as text. The string "\n" supplies a newline; print instead produces an R-style representation that can include index labels such as [1].

These fixtures run on R 4.5.0 with available base packages. Current official release manuals describe a newer release; this course does not claim the installed runtime is the latest version. The app is a concept reader, not an R browser runner.

foundations.reasoning: Rscript evaluates the saved file; a GUI and manual compilation are not required.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace the second value with "two". What type is reported?

essentialSupport.fact: c(1, 2) combines values into an atomic vector. Its elements share a common storage type; c is a function call, not a declaration of separate scalar variables.
Combining numeric values with text converts this atomic vector to character data. Logical values can be converted to numbers when combined with numeric values.
typeof(values) returns the storage type name. This is distinct from class, which can describe higher-level behavior such as a factor or data frame.

foundations.reasoning: This c call produces a single common atomic type; the character element makes the result character.

foundations.quizTarget: Remove L from 1L. What type prints?

essentialSupport.fact: 1 is normally a double-precision numeric value in R, even though it looks like a whole number.
1L creates an integer value. typeof distinguishes integer from double; both can participate in numeric calculations.
Double precision cannot represent every real number exactly. Integer storage has a finite range; neither type is an unlimited exact arithmetic guarantee.

foundations.reasoning: R normally represents an unsuffixed numeric literal as double.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace c(10,20) with the single value 10. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: For equal-length numeric vectors, + adds corresponding positions rather than concatenating them.
c(1,2,3,4) + c(10,20) repeats the shorter vector to match four positions. A non-multiple length can warn; a warning is not a validation policy.
Adding 10 to this vector adds ten to every entry. For unrelated data, check lengths explicitly instead of relying on accidental recycling.
cat(result, sep=",") prints entries separated by commas. sep controls formatting, not the calculation.

foundations.reasoning: The shorter operand now has one value, so every element receives the same increment.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace the right operand TRUE with FALSE. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: c(TRUE,FALSE) is a two-element logical vector. NA can represent an unknown logical value.
& and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.

if needs one non-missing logical result. A scalar numeric value can be coerced to logical, but explicit comparisons make intent clearer. It does not choose a policy for an entire vector or an unknown value.

foundations.reasoning: Elementwise AND with FALSE is false at both positions.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the index vector to c(2,3). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: values[1] selects the first element, not the second. Brackets request a subset.
values[c(1,3)] selects the first and third entries, in that requested order. Repeating an index can repeat an entry.
For this simple atomic vector, an absent positive position yields NA. Other extraction operators have different rules, taught later.

foundations.reasoning: R uses one-based positions and preserves the requested index order.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace -1 with c(-1,2). What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: values[-1] selects all entries except the first. It does not mean the final element as it does in some languages.
A zero index contributes no selected element. It can appear with negative indices without selecting anything.
A subscript vector containing both a positive and a negative nonzero index is rejected. Choose either selection or omission consistently.

foundations.reasoning: The requested subscript mixes incompatible selection styles instead of identifying a valid subset.

foundations.quizTarget: Add the explicit !is.na(values) & check to the mask. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A mask from values > 2 selects elements whose comparison is TRUE. A comparison involving NA normally produces NA.
Indexing an atomic vector with an NA mask entry includes a missing result at that position. Unknown does not silently mean false.

is.na(values) marks missing entries. ! negates those flags. Combining !is.na(values) & (values > 2) rejects missing entries while retaining known qualifying values. Both masks are evaluated elementwise: & is not short-circuiting, and FALSE & NA is FALSE.

foundations.reasoning: The combined mask is FALSE at the missing position and TRUE only for the known qualifying value.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the requested name from "b" to "x". What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: names(values) <- c("a","b") labels the two positions. Labels do not alter their stored numeric values.
values["b"] selects the entry named b. A name is not the same thing as its position number.
For this bracket lookup, an absent name produces NA. Do not assume a misspelled name selects the first entry.

foundations.reasoning: The requested label is absent, so this atomic-vector lookup produces a missing result.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace is.na with is.finite. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: NA represents missing information. NaN represents an undefined numeric result. Inf and -Inf represent positive and negative infinity.
is.na is TRUE for NA and NaN, but FALSE for Inf and ordinary finite values. Comparing a value with NA does not establish whether it is missing.
is.finite is TRUE only for finite numeric values, so it is FALSE for NA, NaN and infinities.

foundations.reasoning: The finite-value predicate excludes missing, undefined and infinite numeric values.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace NULL with NA. What length prints?

essentialSupport.fact: NULL is a special null object with length zero. NA is a missing value that can occupy an element position.
numeric(0) creates an empty double vector, whereas character(0) creates empty text storage. Both have length zero but are not identical types.
length reports how many entries an object contains; it is not the amount of text used to print the object.

foundations.reasoning: NA is a length-one missing value here, unlike the length-zero NULL object.

foundations.quizTarget: Add collapse="|" to the paste0 call. What length prints?

essentialSupport.fact: c("a","b") contains two text elements, not a single string with a comma.
paste0("item", c(1,2)) produces two character elements: item1 and item2. Numeric values are converted to text for this operation.
collapse="|" joins the resulting elements with a vertical bar. Without collapse, the result can still contain several strings.

foundations.reasoning: collapse combines the result entries into a single character element; length counts elements, not characters.

foundations.quizTarget: Change items[1] to items[[1]]. What type prints?

essentialSupport.fact: list(score=7, topic="stars") stores a number and text as separate components without forcing one common atomic type.
items[1] returns a one-component list. items[[1]] extracts the component itself. That extracted component can be a vector or another complex object.
items$score is convenient for a fixed component name. For programmatically supplied exact names, [[ with an explicit name is clearer than relying on partial matching.

foundations.reasoning: The first component is the numeric literal 7, stored as a double; [[ removes the selected outer list level.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the requested row to 2 while keeping the score column. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: data.frame(topic=c("a","b"), score=c(2,4)) combines two columns. Columns may have different types while each describes the same number of rows.
frame[1, "score"] selects row 1 from the score column. An empty row position means all rows; row and column positions are not interchangeable.
frame$score extracts that column. A row normally combines observations across several columns, rather than being a single variable.

foundations.reasoning: Both row and column selectors contribute to the result; the column stays score and the row changes.

foundations.quizTarget: Remove drop=FALSE. What class prints for this numeric column?

essentialSupport.fact: Selecting one data-frame column with frame[, "score"] normally simplifies to the underlying vector.
frame[, "score", drop=FALSE] keeps a one-column data frame. The values are the same, but the container shape differs.
A function expecting row/column structure can behave differently when given a vector. Do not infer shape only from the printed numbers.

foundations.reasoning: The default subset behavior drops the one-column data-frame structure in this expression.

foundations.quizTarget: Convert to character before numeric: as.numeric(as.character(value)). What prints for these labels?

essentialSupport.fact: factor(c("20","10"), levels=c("10","20")) stores category labels with integer codes determined by the level order.
as.numeric(factor_value) exposes the underlying category codes. It does not parse the printed category labels as numbers.
as.character first obtains the labels. as.numeric can then parse valid numeric text; unsuitable text can produce NA with a warning, so real input still needs validation.

foundations.reasoning: The intermediate character conversion obtains the displayed labels, separating label parsing from category-code access.

foundations.quizTarget: Add byrow=TRUE when creating the matrix. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: matrix(c(1,2,3,4), nrow=2) creates a two-row matrix. An array generalizes dimensions beyond rows and columns.
With byrow=FALSE, the first column receives 1 and 2, then the second receives 3 and 4. byrow=TRUE fills rows instead.
m[1,2] reads row 1, column 2. Changing the fill order changes where input values are placed, not the meaning of the two indices.

foundations.reasoning: Row-wise filling places 2 at row 1, column 2.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace values with numeric(0). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: for (index in seq_along(values)) visits each valid position of this vector. It does not require a separate manual counter update.
seq_along(numeric(0)) is an empty index sequence. The colon operator makes a sequence including both endpoints. Thus 1:length(values) becomes 1:0 for empty input, which is not an empty sequence.
numeric(length(values)) can allocate a result vector before a loop. Avoid repeatedly growing large vectors without measuring the cost.
count <- count + 1 updates the local count once per iteration. The starting zero remains zero if the sequence is empty.

foundations.reasoning: seq_along avoids the empty-input trap of 1:length and produces no iterations.

foundations.quizTarget: Supply offset=-1 as an additional named argument. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: function(score, offset=1) declares a required score and a default offset. Named arguments can be supplied explicitly rather than relying on position.
The last evaluated expression supplies the result unless return exits earlier. Returning a value is distinct from printing it.
R supports several argument-matching rules, including partial matching in some situations. Exact names are clearer and less vulnerable to future parameter additions.

foundations.reasoning: The function evaluates 3 plus the supplied -1 rather than using the omitted-argument default.

foundations.quizTarget: Remove the inner value <- 9 assignment. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A function can read a value from the environment where it was created when no local binding shadows it. This is lexical lookup, not a search through every caller’s local variables.
value <- 9 in this function does not automatically overwrite the outer value. The super-assignment operator <<- has different effects and is not used here.
The function returns its final local value. cat prints that result followed by the outer value, separated by a comma.

foundations.reasoning: Without a local value binding, lookup reaches the outer environment; reading it does not modify it.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Insert force(x) as the first statement of choose. What happens for the same call?

essentialSupport.fact: A supplied function argument is usually a promise: its expression and calling environment are retained until the value is needed. An unused argument can therefore contain an expression that would fail if evaluated. stop(message) raises an error and interrupts normal execution.
force(x) evaluates the promise for x now. It is useful before returning a closure that should retain the current argument value. It does not recursively force every promise stored elsewhere.

functions-and-data.reasoning: force makes the stop expression run even though the later if branch would not otherwise use x.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace remove = TRUE with rem = 1. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: ... collects arguments not matched to other formal parameters and can forward them into another call. sum(..., na.rm = remove) passes those values to sum and separately sets its missing-value policy.

Formal parameters after ... must be matched by their exact names. Partial names are not matched to remove here. sum adds numeric values; without na.rm = TRUE, a missing value makes this result missing. A numeric argument accidentally captured by ... becomes data, not an option.

functions-and-data.reasoning: rem is captured in ... rather than matching remove. remove stays FALSE, so the NA is not removed.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Remove force(amount), keeping the later base <- 9. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A closure combines a function with the environment where it was defined. The returned function can still find amount in the completed make_adder call’s environment.

force(amount) evaluates the supplied base expression while base is 2. Without forcing before return, the retained promise can evaluate that expression later, after the caller changes base. A closure retains bindings and environments, not automatically frozen snapshots of all names.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The unforced promise evaluates base when add first needs amount, so it obtains 9 and adds 3.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace new.env(parent = emptyenv()) with list(). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: new.env creates an environment, a mutable mapping from names to values. Assigning it to alias does not copy the environment; both names refer to the same bindings. $ reads or assigns a named binding in this example.

parent = emptyenv() makes this a data-only environment with no inherited bindings. Ordinary lists use value-like copy-on-modify behavior, while environments are intentionally shared. Do not infer that changing any R object through an alias always updates the original.

functions-and-data.reasoning: Updating the list through alias does not change the original state list, unlike updating the shared environment binding.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change the unit attribute to hours. Does the numeric storage convert?

essentialSupport.fact: attr(x, name) reads a named attribute; assigning through it attaches metadata. Attributes can record names, dimensions, class or a custom unit. This custom unit label does not itself convert numbers or enforce a unit system.

typeof reports the underlying R type. class reports the class used by many higher-level operations; setting a class label does not validate that the object satisfies its intended contract. Special attributes can alter interpretation without replacing the stored numbers.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The custom unit attribute is metadata, not executable conversion logic.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change class = "minutes" to class = "other". What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: UseMethod("describe") selects a method according to the class of the generic’s first argument. describe.minutes names a method for the minutes class; describe.default is the fallback when no matching class method is found.

structure(5, class = "minutes") creates the value with a class attribute. This S3 tag is informal: production constructors must check their own invariants. Call the generic rather than guessing a method name at each call site.

functions-and-data.reasoning: No describe.other method exists, so dispatch reaches describe.default.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace minutes = 5 with minutes = "five". What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: S4 classes can declare named slots and their classes. methods::setClass defines StudyEntry with a numeric minutes slot. package::name accesses an exported function from that installed package without attaching it to the search path; methods is part of this R installation.

methods::new constructs an S4 object and checks its declared representation. entry@minutes accesses the slot. A numeric slot does not by itself require positive minutes; domain constraints need a validity rule or explicit validation.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The declared numeric slot does not accept a character value. Declaring structure catches this mismatch, though it does not validate every domain rule.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change read_minutes(0) to read_minutes(3). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: tryCatch evaluates an expression and uses a matching handler when a condition is signaled. error = function(e) receives the error object; its return value becomes the tryCatch result. The failed function does not resume at its next statement.

Here -1 is a deliberate sentinel outside the allowed positive domain. Real code can instead return a structured result with status and message. Catch errors only where you can handle them; blanket fallback values can hide defects.

functions-and-data.reasoning: No error is raised for 3, so the normal function result is returned and the handler is unused.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace withCallingHandlers with tryCatch, and replace invokeRestart("muffleWarning") with 9. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: warning signals a condition but normally allows evaluation to continue. withCallingHandlers runs a matching handler in the signaling context. This differs from tryCatch’s exiting handler, which abandons that expression’s remaining normal path.

invokeRestart("muffleWarning") invokes the restart provided by warning to suppress its default reporting after the handler has recorded it. This is not blanket suppression of all failures. The returned result still comes from the code after warning.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The tryCatch warning handler exits the expression and supplies 9, so the following 4 is not evaluated.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change work() to work(TRUE). What prints after the error is caught?

essentialSupport.fact: on.exit records an expression to run when the current function exits normally or through an error. Register cleanup as soon as a resource or temporary state needs restoring. add = TRUE adds a cleanup expression instead of replacing an earlier one.

The on.exit expression here restores a shared environment binding; it does not replace the normal return value. Cleanup can itself fail, so keep it reliable and avoid masking the original failure. This example changes only a local fixture environment, not global configuration.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The error triggers the handler’s -1, but function exit still runs the registered restoration to FALSE.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace sum with function(x) x, keeping numeric(1). What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: lapply returns one list element per input element, preserving a list result even when values are simple. vapply additionally requires each function result to match an explicit length and compatible type template.

numeric(1) is a length-one double template here. Each sum returns one numeric total. vapply may promote compatible simpler types, but it rejects an incompatible result length or type rather than silently choosing a different output shape as sapply can.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The identity function returns each two-element vector, violating the one-element template.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change the margin from 1 to 2. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: apply(m, 1, sum) applies sum to each row; margin 2 selects columns. Matrix filling is column-major by default, so these rows contain 1,3,5 and 2,4,6.

apply operates on arrays and may convert a data frame to a matrix first. Mixing character and numeric columns can therefore coerce all cells to text. For plain numeric totals, rowSums or colSums are more direct; apply is not automatically faster than every explicit alternative.

functions-and-data.reasoning: Columns are (1,2), (3,4) and (5,6), so their sums are 3, 7 and 11.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change na.rm = TRUE to na.rm = FALSE. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: split(values, groups) returns a list of vectors, one per grouping level. Here a contains 2 and NA while b contains 6. Equal-length input and group vectors avoid unintended recycling; missing group labels need an explicit policy.

mean averages a numeric vector. na.rm = TRUE removes missing observations for each group; an all-missing group can produce NaN rather than an informative average. Removing missing observations changes which data support each estimate, so record counts as well when needed.

functions-and-data.reasoning: Group a contains an NA and now propagates it; group b has no missing value and remains 6.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Remove scores from order(keys, scores). What changes in the first line?

essentialSupport.fact: order(keys, scores) returns row positions sorted by keys, breaking equal-key ties with scores. For this default ordering, unresolved ties retain their original relative order. Apply the same index to every aligned column; sorting one column alone breaks row relationships.

duplicated marks occurrences after the first equal value. It does not automatically merge or remove all rows belonging to repeated keys. To detect a nonunique key policy, use those flags deliberately rather than assuming sorting removes duplicates.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The equal a keys retain their original order when no score tie-breaker is supplied, so scores 3 and 2 precede b’s 1.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace the right table with one row id = 1, label = "a". How many joined rows remain?

essentialSupport.fact: merge(left, right, by = "id") combines rows with equal id values. Its default is an inner join: unmatched keys are omitted. all.x = TRUE retains unmatched left rows with missing right-side values.

Repeated keys can create multiple row pairs: two matching left rows and two matching right rows produce four joined rows. Validate key uniqueness when your model expects one-to-one or many-to-one relationships. Do not silently interpret duplicated joins as new independent observations.

functions-and-data.reasoning: Each of the two left rows now has exactly one matching right row.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change the day labels times = c(1, 2) to times = c(10, 20). What changes in the printed row count and sum?

essentialSupport.fact: A wide table stores day1 and day2 in separate columns. A long table stores a day identifier and one minutes column, with repeated id values. This changes the layout, not the underlying measurements.

reshape uses varying for the measurement columns, v.names for their shared value name, timevar and times for the new occasion labels, and idvar for the entity identifier. direction = "long" selects this conversion. Verify unique entity/occasion pairs before trying a reverse wide transformation.

functions-and-data.reasoning: times supplies occasion labels rather than multipliers or repetition counts, so the same four values remain.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change na.rm = TRUE to na.rm = FALSE. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: The native |> pipe normally inserts its left expression as the first argument of the call on the right. This expression is equivalent to sum(c(1, NA, 3), na.rm = TRUE); it is ordinary R syntax, not a package dependency.

To place the value explicitly in a named argument, a named _ placeholder can be used once in an eligible call, such as value |> round(x = _, digits = 1). A pipe does not automatically vectorize a scalar-only function or change its missing-value behavior.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The pipe only places the vector into sum; the explicit missing-value policy still controls the result.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Remove fixed = TRUE from both calls. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: grepl returns one logical match result per input string. With fixed = TRUE the dot is literal; without it, dot is a regular-expression wildcard matching a character. Know which interpretation your input needs.

gsub replaces every match and returns strings; sub replaces only the first match in each string. Neither evaluates the replacement as R code. Complex regular expressions and unbounded external input need separate performance and validation limits.

functions-and-data.reasoning: The dot now matches each character, so both strings match and all three characters in each become hyphens.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Change instant + 3600 to instant + 1. What time prints on the second line?

essentialSupport.fact: as.Date represents calendar dates, and adding a number adds days. as.POSIXct represents instants; adding a number adds seconds. Specify a time zone when parsing clock text to avoid relying on the session’s local zone.

format turns values into display strings. %Y-%m-%d selects a date and %H:%M selects hours and minutes. Regional daylight-saving rules mean one calendar day is not always 86400 elapsed seconds; the fixture uses UTC deliberately and does not assert regional behavior.

functions-and-data.reasoning: One second advances to 00:30:01; the format omits seconds, so the displayed minute stays 00:30.

functions-and-data.quizTarget: Replace stats::median with median in the last line. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: library attaches an installed package’s exported names to the search path. Another binding can mask an unqualified name. package::name selects that package’s exported object directly without attaching all of its names; it does not install a missing package.

stats is included in this R installation. Its median selects the middle ordered value for this odd-length vector. A local function named median can coexist with stats::median. Avoid package:::internal as an application contract: unexported internals may change. Record R and package versions; do not assume an attached package implies the latest release.

functions-and-data.reasoning: Both unqualified calls now resolve to the local function, whereas the qualified call bypassed that masking.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If both declared column classes become numeric, how is ID 001 printed?

essentialSupport.fact: read.csv reads delimited text into a data frame. Here text supplies a tiny literal CSV rather than an external path. colClasses declares the ID as character and minutes as numeric, so leading zeros in an identifier are not mistaken for numeric magnitude.

An imported column still needs its meaning, missing-value policy and valid range checked. stringsAsFactors = FALSE makes the intended text treatment explicit. Never assume a plausible inferred type proves that units, IDs or measurements were interpreted correctly.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The numeric conversion retains magnitude but not leading-zero formatting; an ID should have remained character.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If minutes changes to 20 before saving, what returns after reading?

essentialSupport.fact: saveRDS writes one R object, preserving R-specific structure such as classes and attributes; readRDS returns the object instead of choosing a variable name in the caller. Assign its result explicitly. This differs from a plain-text CSV interchange.

The fixture writes and reads its own local object. RDS is not a safe interchange boundary for arbitrary untrusted files and is not guaranteed portable forever across versions or systems. Validate the loaded shape and record provenance; do not execute unknown serialized content as a substitute for a documented data format.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The serialized object contains the updated numeric field; reading reconstructs that saved object rather than an earlier variable state.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the text passed to write_note changes to rest, what is read after it returns?

essentialSupport.fact: A connection represents an input or output stream. file(path, open = "wt") opens a text-writing connection; close releases it. Inside a function, on.exit(close(con), add = TRUE) registers cleanup even if the body errors.

file.path joins path components using platform conventions, not an authorization policy. writeLines writes text lines to the connection; readLines reads them after the writer is closed. The example owns a disposable relative path and never accepts a user-supplied traversal path.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Cleanup closes the stream but does not roll back or delete the completed file; the new line remains available to read.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the expected value becomes 0.4 with the same tiny tolerance, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: Floating-point arithmetic can differ from ideal decimal arithmetic. all.equal compares approximately but returns either TRUE or a descriptive character result, not simply FALSE on mismatch. Wrap it in isTRUE for a single logical condition.

stopifnot stops when a supplied condition is not TRUE. Use tolerance appropriate to the quantity and its scale, not a tolerance so large that a wrong result passes. This arithmetic check is not a statistical uncertainty interval.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: A difference of about 0.1 is far beyond the stated tolerance, so isTRUE is false and the assertion stops execution.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If both sample sizes change to 2, which properties hold?

essentialSupport.fact: set.seed initializes the random-number generator state. sample selects values, with replace = FALSE giving sampling without replacement. unique removes duplicate values, so length(unique(first)) counts distinct sampled values. Resetting the same seed before the same operation reproduces its sequence in the same relevant runtime/RNG configuration.

A fixed seed does not make a convenience sample unbiased or make simulated data real evidence. Record R and RNG versions for reproducibility, and do not compare only one random outcome to justify a method. Here equality is checked rather than relying on an unexplained fixed random vector.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Both runs reset the same seed and use the same new size; without replacement, the two selected values are distinct.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the last value becomes 90, what changes?

essentialSupport.fact: mean adds values and divides by count; median is the middle ordered value, averaging the two central values for even length. Extreme values can move the mean substantially while leaving the median relatively stable.

An outlier is not automatically an error to delete. Check units, collection process and the intended population before choosing exclusions. These values are synthetic minutes and only illustrate arithmetic; neither summary alone describes the whole distribution.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The sum increases by 40 across four observations, moving the mean by ten; the two middle ordered values remain ten.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If every value is multiplied by 2, what happens to sd and IQR?

essentialSupport.fact: sprintf("%.1f", x) formats a number as text with one decimal place; it changes display, not the stored number. sd estimates sample standard deviation using denominator n - 1; its unit matches the observations. var is its square and has squared units. quantile estimates cut points; R supports several definitions, so type = 7 is explicit here.

IQR is the difference between upper and lower quartiles. Multiplying all observations by a constant scales sd and IQR by its absolute value and variance by its square. For very small samples, spread estimates are unstable and conventions matter. Removing missing values changes the observations summarized and must follow a stated policy, not merely silence NA output.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Both standard deviation and quantile differences scale with absolute multiplicative scale; variance, not sd, would quadruple.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If both threshold and mean change to 20, with sd still 2, what is the cumulative probability?

essentialSupport.fact: R commonly uses d for density or mass, p for cumulative probability, q for quantiles and r for random generation. pnorm(q, mean, sd) gives the probability at or below q under a specified normal model; a continuous density value is not the probability of one exact point.

A nondegenerate normal model is symmetric around its mean and has positive standard deviation; R also supports the special sd = 0 point-mass boundary, which is not used here. A calculation under that model does not establish that a real dataset is normal. Here the threshold equals the model mean, so half the probability lies below it.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Normal symmetry depends on position relative to the mean, not the absolute numeric location.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the other confidence level becomes 0.90 instead of 0.99, is it wider than the 0.95 interval?

essentialSupport.fact: t.test(x)$conf.int gives a t-based interval for a population mean. Under its sampling/model assumptions, a 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true mean in 95% of repeated samples; it is not a statement that 95% of individual future values lie in this realized interval.

For the same data and method, a higher confidence level produces a wider interval. The method depends on independent observations and a suitable mean-sampling model, especially with tiny samples. Synthetic numbers here demonstrate the computation, not scientific adequacy.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Holding data and method fixed, the lower critical value for 90% confidence produces a narrower mean interval, not an individual prediction interval.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If mu becomes 0 for this same sample, which claim follows from a TRUE threshold check?

essentialSupport.fact: A one-sample t.test compares a mean with mu under its model assumptions. The p-value is the probability, under the null model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; it is not the probability that the null is true or that a result happened by chance.

Here the sample mean equals the tested null mean, producing p = 1. A threshold comparison alone is not practical importance, a causal conclusion or proof of no effect. Consider design, independence, distributional assumptions, multiple testing and effect size; five synthetic values do not validate a real study.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Moving the null mean to zero yields a more extreme standardized difference for these data; the threshold is still a model-conditional test result, not a causal or posterior probability statement.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If y is negated, what correlation and causal conclusion follow?

essentialSupport.fact: cor(x, y) defaults to Pearson correlation, a unitless measure of linear association between paired observations. It ranges from -1 to 1 when defined; zero variance or unsuitable missingness handling can make a calculation undefined or misleading.

A strong correlation can arise from confounding, reverse direction or design artifacts. Do not infer that changing x causes y to change. The constructed straight-line data isolate sign, not real-world validity; inspect shape and sampling context in actual analysis.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Negating one variable reverses the direction of the exact linear association; neither sign establishes a causal mechanism.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If every y value is doubled, how do the intercept and slope change?

essentialSupport.fact: lm(y ~ x, data = data) fits a linear response model with an intercept and x term by least squares. The tilde separates response from predictors; + adds terms in a formula, and y ~ 1 is an intercept-only model rather than the arithmetic assignment y = 1.

coef extracts fitted coefficients: intercept first and x slope next here. The slope describes a fitted change in mean y per unit x under the model, not automatically a causal effect. With the predictor design fixed, multiplying every response by a constant multiplies all least-squares coefficients by that constant. Tiny synthetic data can demonstrate fitting without validating the linear-model assumptions.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Least-squares coefficients scale with the response when the design is unchanged; the formula does not prescribe the numeric slope.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If chosen uses interval = "prediction", what does the width comparison show?

essentialSupport.fact: predict.lm with interval = "confidence" estimates uncertainty about the conditional mean response. interval = "prediction" additionally accounts for variation in one future observation under the fitted model, so it is wider here. Both depend on assumptions, not just successful software execution.

newdata supplies predictor values in a data frame. Its x = 3 is inside the observed range 1..5. Predictions far outside that range can be scientifically unreliable even if R returns a number. The returned matrix has fit, lwr and upr columns.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: A prediction interval adds residual observation variation, so it is wider for this nonzero-residual fit; it is not a guarantee about any one future outcome.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the formula becomes y ~ x - 1, must residuals still sum to zero?

essentialSupport.fact: residuals(fit) extracts discrepancies between responses and fitted means. In ordinary least squares with an intercept, their sum is approximately zero by the fitting equations; that arithmetic property is not evidence that every modeling assumption holds.

Residual-versus-fitted patterns may suggest nonlinearity or unequal variance; a Q-Q plot can reveal departures from a normal-error model. Checks cannot prove independence, exclude confounding or certify a small sample. In an R model formula, - 1 removes the intercept. Removing the intercept changes the zero-sum property, not just a display label.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The intercept normal equation enforces the zero-sum property; removing that term removes that constraint. A failed arithmetic property is not by itself a scientific diagnosis.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the reference becomes B, what are the intercept and A-versus-B coefficient?

essentialSupport.fact: A factor represents categories, not the numeric magnitudes of its internal codes. Under treatment contrasts, the first level is the reference: the intercept is its fitted group mean and the other coefficient is a difference from that mean.

factor(levels = c("A", "B")) and an explicit contr.treatment setting make coding visible. relevel changes the reference category, changing coefficient interpretation without changing the fitted group means. These group differences are descriptive, not automatically effects of an intervention.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: B has mean seven, and A is four lower; changing reference recodes the same fitted group means.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If type becomes link, is the printed -1.099 a negative probability?

essentialSupport.fact: glm with family = binomial() uses the logit link by default for a binary response. A 0/1 vector records failures/successes. The linear predictor is log-odds, log(p / (1 - p)); it is not itself a probability.

predict(type = "response") converts the linear predictor to probabilities, while type = "link" returns log-odds here. This intercept-only example estimates one shared probability. Separation, convergence, sample size and calibration matter in real models; four synthetic outcomes cannot validate risk predictions.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The link scale is unbounded and can be negative; transforming back through the inverse logit gives a probability between zero and one.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the y-axis label changes to Seconds without converting the values, what changes?

essentialSupport.fact: pdf opens a headless file graphics device; plot sends drawing commands to the active device. dev.off closes it and finalizes the PDF. A function with on.exit(dev.off(), add = TRUE) makes cleanup occur even if plotting fails.

The fixture creates one synthetic scatterplot in plot.pdf. main is its title; xlab and ylab are axis labels; pch chooses a point symbol. No GUI display, browser execution or publication is implied. Check the generated artifact rather than treating printed success as visual verification.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: Axis text documents intended units but performs no unit conversion; changing it alone can mislabel the data.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If breaks become c(0, 1, 4), what bin counts result?

essentialSupport.fact: hist bins a numeric distribution, boxplot summarizes center/spread and flagged extremes, and plot(x, y) shows paired values. par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) arranges three panels; it changes layout rather than the data.

With explicit equal-width breaks and right = TRUE, bins are right-closed; include.lowest includes the lowest endpoint. For unequal-width breaks, hist defaults to density so bar areas, not raw heights, represent proportions. The example compares bin counts, not just a decorative image. Boxplot flagged points are not automatically bad data, and scatterplot association is not causation.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The first interval contains one and the second contains two, three and four. The altered bins are unequal-width, so density rather than raw bar height is needed for a distribution display.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If n changes to 100, which claim is supported?

essentialSupport.fact: system.time evaluates an expression and reports measured CPU and elapsed time. Rprof samples execution for profiling, and Rprof(NULL) stops profiling. Short work may produce no useful samples; timings vary by runtime, load and hardware, so this example never asserts a specific duration or speedup.

Profiling identifies where time is spent, not which result is correct. Compare outputs and representative workloads before changing algorithms; warm-up and repeated measurements may matter. This bounded example writes a local profile file and verifies only the computed result plus a nonnegative elapsed measurement.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The workload now sums integers one through one hundred; elapsed measurements include variable overhead and cannot be predicted as an exact scale factor.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If context$x becomes 9 before eval, what value results?

essentialSupport.fact: quote captures an R expression without evaluating it. eval evaluates that expression in a supplied environment; new.env(parent = baseenv()) gives this example a controlled lookup context for a known expression, not a security sandbox.

The expression here is authored directly as x + 1 and x is explicitly bound. Parsing arbitrary text and evaluating it can run arbitrary R operations; an environment or an allowlist of variable names alone does not make unknown code safe. Prefer a data format and explicit operations for external input.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: quote stored the expression rather than an evaluated numeric result; eval resolves x in the given context at evaluation time.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If temporary digits becomes 5, does it leak after the function returns?

essentialSupport.fact: sessionInfo records the R version, platform and loaded package information. RNGkind describes random-generator configuration; options can also affect behavior and formatting. Saving metadata helps explain a run but does not by itself recreate dependencies, input data or operating-system behavior.

options returns prior values for changed settings, so a function can register on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE). This keeps local formatting from leaking into later analysis. Rscript --vanilla avoids startup files and workspace restoration, but still needs explicit data, package versions and seed policy.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: The saved prior settings are reapplied on exit; digits is display configuration rather than a transformation of stored values.

analysis-and-graphics.quizTarget: If the first value becomes 65, what is retained and summarized?

essentialSupport.fact: A bounded pipeline checks type, missingness and domain before summarizing. Here input is a finite numeric vector; is.finite excludes NA, NaN and infinities, and the accepted range is 1..60 minutes. head(valid, 3) caps the number of retained valid observations.

The retained count and arithmetic mean describe only accepted observations in this synthetic input. They do not establish a population mean, causality or real-world validity. Real analysis also needs units, provenance, input-size limits and an explicit exclusion policy; silently dropping data can bias conclusions.

analysis-and-graphics.reasoning: 65 and 70 exceed the upper bound, zero is below it and NA is nonfinite; only twenty passes the stated policy.
